"Pakistani PL-15 missile strikes down an Indian Rafale jet near Bahawalpur, destroying and burning it to ashes. Single-seater. Pilot confirmed dead. Let this be a lesson: don't challenge Pakistan's skies," read the post's caption that garnered 6,140 views. Here is the link and archive link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. Investigation The Desk ran the viral photo through Reverse Image Search and found that other users shared the same picture with a similar claim on social media. One such post can be found here , and its archived version can be viewed here . On further scanning the search results, the Desk came across a Times of India report published on May 21, 2021, featuring the same image as seen in the viral post. According to the report, a MiG-21 fighter jet of the Indian Air Force (IAF) crashed in the fields near Langeana Khurd village of Moga district in Punjab. The pilot, Squadron Leader Abhinav Choudhary, died in the crash. Here is the link to the report, and below is a screenshot of the same. Below is a combination image highlighting the similarities between the viral photo and the article's feature image. Taking a cue from this, the Desk conducted a customised keyword search on Google to find relevant media reports. It came across a Press Trust of India (PTI) report carried by Business Standard published on May 21, 2021. The report citing officials said the aircraft was on a routine sortie from Suratgarh when it crashed near a village in Moga. "Indian Air Force pilot killed as MiG-21 Bison aircraft crashes in Punjab," read the headline of the report. Here is the link to the report, and below is a screenshot of the same. A statement was also issued by the Indian Air Force on May 21, 2021, stating that the pilot, Sqn Ldr Abhinav Choudhary, sustained fatal injuries in the aircraft accident. "There was an aircraft accident last night involving a Bison aircraft of the IAF in the western sector. The pilot, Sqn Ldr Abhinav Choudhary, sustained fatal injuries. IAF condoles the tragic loss and stands firmly with the bereaved family," read the statement. Here is the link , and below is a screenshot of the same. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the viral photo dates back to 2021 when a MiG-21 fighter jet of the Indian Air Force (IAF) crashed in the fields near Langeana Khurd village of Moga district in Punjab. It led to Sqn. Ldr Abhinav Choudhary sustaining fatal injuries. It is unrelated to Operation Sindoor. Claim 5: A video featuring a massive blast with sirens wailing in the background was shared by an X user named '𝗕𝗮𝗿𝗿𝘆 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗼𝗻 𝗥𝗲𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗻' on May 7, claiming that Pakistan fired missiles into the Indian territory. Pakistan has fired multiple missiles into Indian territory. New visuals indicate that the situation is becoming increasingly volatile," read the post's caption that clocked 2,768 views. Here is the link and archive link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. Investigation: The Desk ran the viral video through the InVid verification tool and extracted multiple keyframes. One of these keyframes was reverse-searched using Google Lens, which led the Desk to several social media posts sharing the same video with similar claims. One such post can be found here , and its archived version can be found here . On further analysis of the search results, the Desk came across an Instagram post dated June 21, 2024, indicating that the video predated Operation Sindoor. Though no additional details were available with the video, it is not recent and unrelated to the recent incident. Here is the link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. Below is a combination image highlighting the similarities between the viral video and the Instagram post. Though the Desk could not verify the source or the incident in the viral video, it is clear that it is not from the recent Operation Sindoor. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the viral video has been available online since 2024, which predates Operation Sindoor. The viral video was shared with a false claim on social media.

author: Vaidehi Jahagirdar/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: These 5 videos circulated after India's 'Operation Sindoor' old and recycled; social media posts shared with misleading claims
content: New Delhi, May 8 (Vaidehi Jahagirdar/Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): Following India's launch of Operation Sindoor on May 7—targeting nine terror-linked sites in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir in response to the Pahalgam terror attack—social media was flooded with misleading videos falsely claiming to show Pakistan's retaliatory actions. Several of these videos were amplified by Pakistan-based propaganda handles and accompanied by fabricated narratives, fueling an online misinformation campaign seemingly aimed at undermining India's official version of events. The PTI Fact Check Desk investigated five such viral posts that attempted to mislead the public by sharing old or unrelated videos and images. Here's a breakdown of each claim and what we found: Claim 1: On May 7, a Pakistan-based handle '@ARYSabirShakir' shared a video on its X account claiming it showed India carried out missile attacks in Bahawalpur Here is the link and archive link to the post, along with a screenshot. Investigation: The Desk ran the viral video through the InVid verification tool and extracted multiple keyframes. One of these keyframes was reverse-searched using Google Lens, which led the Desk to several social media posts sharing the same video with similar claims. Two such posts can be found here and here , with their archived versions viewed here and here , respectively. The reverse image search also led the Desk to a video posted on the X account of the Afghanistan-based Kabul News channel. The channel had posted the same video as seen in the above viral posts, with details suggesting that the footage depicted massive bombing carried out in Gaza by Israeli forces in October 2023. Israel intensified its bombing of Gaza last night. According to Palestinian media reports, 400 people, including women and children, lost their lives in the bombings, and hundreds more are still trapped under collapsed buildings," the Afghan-based channel posted with the video. Here is the link and archive link to the post, along with a screenshot. Below is a combination image highlighting the viral video's content, matched with the video posted by the Afghan-based news channel. Additionally, the Desk conducted a customised keyword search on Google to learn more about the nine terror-linked sites under 'Operation Sindoor' targeted by India. The search led to an X post shared by the Press Trust of India, which confirmed that India targeted one of the terrorist-linked sites in Pakistan's Bahawalpur—Markaz Subhan Allah. However, the video shared in the social media post was not linked to this strike. Here is the link to the post the Press Trust of India shared, along with a screenshot. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the viral video does not depict India's operation in Pakistan's Bahawalpur under 'OPERATION SINDOOR'. Claim 2: A video of an aircraft burnt into ashes was shared by an X user, DR. STRANGER (@hitmayn51), with a claim that it depicted India's Rafale aircraft that was hit by Pakistan's PL-15 BVR missiles near Bahawalpur. The user claimed the pilot had also died in the incident. Here is the link and archive link to the post, along with a screenshot. Investigation: The Desk ran the viral video through the InVid verification tool and extracted multiple keyframes. One of these keyframes was reverse-searched using Google Lens, which led the Desk to several social media posts sharing the same video with similar claims. Two such posts can be found here and here , with their archived versions available here and here , respectively. The reverse image search also led the Desk to a video posted on the official YouTube channel of the Jordan-based Roya News English portal. The channel had posted the exact same video, but the accompanying details revealed it depicted a Pakistan Air Force training aircraft that had crashed in the fields of Ratta Tibba in the suburbs of Vehari on April 16, 2025. Here is the link to the video, along with a screenshot. Below is a combination image highlighting the viral video's content, matched with the video posted by the Afghan-based news channel. In the next part of the investigation, taking cues from the above-generated inputs, the Desk conducted a customised keyword search on Google about the incident. The search led to a report published by the Dawn News portal, which confirmed that the video pertained to the PAF training aircraft crash due to a technical fault in Pakistan's Punjab province. Here is the link to the report, along with a screenshot. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the viral video does not show an Indian aircraft being shot down by Pakistan in Bahawalpur. Claim 3: Pakistan-based X user Ali Imran Abbasi (@aliimranabbasi) posted a video claiming Indian soldiers raised a white flag to collect their fallen near the LoC after a Pakistani Army attack. Here is the link and archive link to the post, along with a screenshot. Investigation: The Desk ran the viral video through the InVid verification tool and extracted multiple keyframes. One of these keyframes was reverse-searched using Google Lens, which led the Desk to several social media posts sharing the same video with similar claims. Two such posts can be found here and here , with their archived versions available here and here , respectively. The reverse image search also led the Desk to a news report published by Zee News, as its feature image matched that of a keyframe from the viral video. Upon analysing the report, the Desk found that the incident showing a white flag raised along the border area depicted Pakistan Army personnel. They did so back in September 2019, to retrieve the bodies of two of its soldiers who the Indian Army killed in retaliation for an unprovoked ceasefire violation. "Troops of the Pakistani Army reached the Hajipur sector in Jammu and Kashmir and retrieved their dead personnel after showing a white flag, a symbol denoting truce or surrender," the report stated. Here is the link to the report, along with a screenshot. Below is a combination image highlighting the viral video's content, matched with that of the feature image of the news report. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the viral video falsely claims the Indian Army raised a white flag at the LoC. Claim 4: On May 7, an X user, Islamist Cannibal (@Raviagrawal300), shared a video of an aircraft taking off at night with a claim that it depicted Pakistani jets flying for a mission against India. Here is the link and archive link to the post, along with a screenshot. Investigation: The Desk ran the viral video through the InVid verification tool and extracted multiple keyframes. One of these keyframes was reverse-searched using Google Lens, which led the Desk to several social media posts sharing the same video with similar claims. Two such posts can be found here and here , with their archived versions available here and here , respectively. The reverse image search also led the Desk to a video published on the YouTube channel 'thecorporatepilotdad'. Upon reviewing it, the Desk found that the footage closely matched the viral video. The accompanying details confirmed that the video was initially posted in December 2023 and does not depict Pakistani jets flying on a mission against India." The video was initially shared with the description, "A pair of F-18s during a night takeoff with full afterburner until just after rotation." Here is the link to the video, along with a screenshot. Below is a combination image highlighting the viral video's content, matched with the video posted by the Afghan-based news channel. While, the Desk could not independently verify had where the video was originally shot, but based on the investigation it concluded that the viral video does not show any Pakistani jets flying for a mission against India amid 'OPERATION SINDOOR'. Claim 5: On May 7, an X user '@VijayaReddy_R' shared a video depicting India's precision strike against Pakistan under 'OPERATION SINDOOR'. Here is the link and archive link to the post, along with a screenshot. Investigation: The Desk ran the viral video through the InVid verification tool and extracted multiple keyframes. One of these keyframes was reverse-searched using Google Lens, which led the Desk to several social media posts sharing the same video with similar claims. Two such posts can be found here and here , with their archived versions viewed here and here : The reverse image search also led the Desk to a post by journalist Baker Atyani on X. He shared the same video, stating that it depicted a November 2023 incident in which an Indonesian hospital in Gaza came under Israeli attack. The video does not depict India's retaliatory strike against Pakistan. Here is the link to the post, along with a screenshot: Below is a combination image highlighting the content in the viral video, which matches the video posted by the X user. To verify further, the Desk conducted a customised keyword search on Google to find relevant media reports. This led to a video report uploaded by Al Jazeera on its official YouTube channel on November 9, 2023. Citing the Palestinian interior ministry, the report mentioned several injuries among thousands of displaced people sheltering in the yard of the Indonesian hospital in northern Gaza. The hospital's vicinity—specifically the Tal al-Zaatar area—was attacked by Israeli fighter jets. The exact footage seen in the viral video appears at the 5-minute 20-second mark in Al Jazeera's report. Here is the link to the video, along with a screenshot. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the viral video dates back to 2023 and showed an Indonesian hospital in Gaza that was under Israeli attack, killing several people. The video predates the launching of 'OPERATION SINDOOR' by Indian Armed forces.

author: Kaushiki Goel/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: 2023 video of Israel striking Gaza falsely shared as Indian Army action in Pakistan during Operation Sindoor
content: New Delhi, May 8 (Kaushiki Goel / Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): Following a decisive strike by the Indian Armed Forces on Wednesday (May 7) under Operation Sindoor, several social media users shared a video showing heavy nighttime bombings, falsely claiming that India had deliberately targeted civilian areas in Pakistan. However, the Press Trust of India's (PTI) Fact Check Desk investigated the claim and found that the viral video actually dates back to 2023, when the Israeli military struck 750 targets in the Gaza Strip. The footage is old and unrelated to India's Operation Sindoor. It was shared on social media with a false claim. Operation Sindoor was launched in response to the April 22 terror attack in Pahalgam, in Jammu and Kashmir's Anantnag district, which killed 26 people—25 Indian nationals and one Nepali citizen. The operation reportedly resulted in the deaths of over 70 terrorists and injuries to more than 60, significantly degrading the operational capability of the terror groups involved. Claim A video featuring massive bombing at night was shared by an X (formerly Twitter) user on May 7, claiming that India is deliberately targeting civilian areas in Pakistan as the Indian Armed Forces executed Operation Sindoor. The post clocked 1.2 million views, and it read: "My relatives in Bahawalpur were asleep when Indian bombs started falling. Why is India deliberately targeting civilian areas in Pakistan?!" Here is the link and archive link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. Investigation The Desk ran the viral video through the InVid verification tool and extracted multiple keyframes. One of these keyframes was reverse-searched using Google Lens, which led the Desk to several social media posts sharing the same video with similar claims. One such post can be found here , and its archived version can be viewed here . On further scanning the search results, the Desk came across an Instagram post dated October 2023, clarifying that it is not recent and unrelated to Operation Sindoor, featuring similar visuals as seen in the viral social media post. Here is the link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. The Desk extracted the keyframes of the viral video and ran them through Reverse Image Search and found an X post by a user named 'Muhammad Smiry' who shared a video similar to the video in October 2023, citing it to be from Gaza. Here is the link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. Taking into considerations the above findings, the Desk conducted a customised keyword search on Google to find relevant media reports and came across report by Sputnik Armenia dated October 13, 2023. The report carried the same video which is being circulated on social media and as per the article it showed Gaza being striked by Israel. "The Israeli army attacked, among other things, underground tunnels, military complexes and posts, as well as the residences of senior Hamas officials. The Israel Defense Forces said it had struck 750 military targets in the Gaza Strip overnight," read a section of the report. Here is the link and archive link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. Below is a combination image highlighting the viral video's content, matched with the video posted by Sputnik Armenia. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the viral video dates back to 2023 when the Israeli army attacked 750 military targets in the Gaza Strip. The video is old and unrelated to the India Forces' Operation Sindoor.

author: Vaidehi Jahagirdar/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: Fire incident video from Mumbai's Dharavi falsely linked to India's Airstrike in Pakistan under Operation Sindoor
content: New Delhi, May 8 (Vaidehi Jahagirdar / Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): A video showing a massive fire erupting on a busy street was recently shared on social media with the claim that it depicted a precision strike by India on Pakistan's Sialkot under Operation Sindoor. However, the PTI Fact Check Desk investigated and found that the video is unrelated to any Indian military action following the Pahalgam terror attack. The footage actually shows a fire that broke out in Mumbai's Dharavi area on March 24, 2025, after multiple cooking gas cylinders packed in a truck caught fire. An unrelated video was falsely shared online, misrepresenting it as evidence of India's military strike under Operation Sindoor. Claim An X (formerly Twitter) handle with the username 'whatever' (@whatever22508) shared a video on May 7, claiming it showed another precision strike carried out by India in Sialkot, Pakistan, under 'Operation Sindoor'. Here is the link and archive link to the post, along with a screenshot. Investigation The Desk ran the viral video through the InVid verification tool and extracted multiple keyframes. One of these keyframes was reverse-searched using Google Lens, which led the Desk to several social media accounts that shared the same video with similar claims. Two such posts can be found here and here , along with their archived versions viewed here and here : The Google reverse image search also led the Desk to a video published on a Facebook page named 'Gulf Digital News - Online'. The video matched the background seen in the viral clip. However, the details shared along with it revealed that the video depicted a blast in Mumbai's Dharavi area caused by multiple cooking gas cylinders in a truck catching fire on March 24, 2025. "Multiple cooking gas cylinders in a truck caught fire and exploded yesterday in Mumbai's biggest slum of Dharavi, local authorities said. The fire was confined to the truck and no injuries were reported," the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation, the city's civic body, stated, according to the Facebook page. Here is the link and archive link to the Facebook post, along with a screenshot: Below is a combination image highlighting that the content seen in the viral video matched that of the video posted by the Facebook page. As part of the investigation, the desk conducted a keyword search on Google to ascertain more details about the cylinder blast in Mumbai's Dharavi region. I came across a report published by the Economic Times on March 25, 2025. The report elaborated on the fire incident, stating that while no injuries or casualties were reported, the situation could have escalated had the truck been parked in a more densely populated area. Over 20 gas cylinders ignited in the incident. Here is the link to the Economic Times report, along with a screenshot: Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the viral video is unrelated to any Indian military operation. It was falsely shared on social media, linking it to India's alleged military strike under 'Operation Sindoor'.

author: Vaidehi Jahagirdar/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: Old jet crash video from Madhya Pradesh falsely shared to claim Pakistani conducted air strike on India; details inside
content: New Delhi, May 8 (Vaidehi Jahagirdar / Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): A video showing an Indian Air Force pilot being rescued by locals after ejecting from a crashed jet was recently circulated on social media with the claim that it depicted a recent Pakistani air strike in response to India's ongoing military operation, Operation Sindoor. The post alleged that the pilot was injured after the Pakistani Air Force intercepted his jet. However, the PTI Fact Check Desk investigated and found that the video is unrelated to any current India-Pakistan military engagement. It actually shows an incident from February 2025, when an Indian Air Force Mirage-2000 fighter jet crashed in Madhya Pradesh's Shivpuri district due to a technical failure. The visuals show the pilot being rescued by locals after safely ejecting from the aircraft. An old, unrelated video was misleadingly shared online and falsely linked to a Pakistani counterstrike following Operation Sindoor. Claim A video shared by an Instagram page named 'talkistanpk' on May 7 claimed that the Pakistani Air Force had intercepted and shot down an Indian fighter jet that had crossed into Pakistani airspace amid ongoing tensions following India's 'Operation Sindoor'. "Pakistani Air Force reportedly intercepted an Indian jet that crossed into Pakistani airspace, injuring the Indian pilot. Situation developing—both sides on alert. Stay tuned for updates," the claim stated along the video read. Here is the link and archive link to the post, along with a screenshot: Investigation The Desk ran the viral video through the InVid tool and extracted multiple keyframes. One of the keyframes was run through Google Lens, which led to multiple users who had also shared the same video with similar captions. Two such posts can be found here and here , with their archived versions viewed here and here , respectively: Next, since the viral video carried an Aaj Tak logo, the Desk conducted a custom keyword search on Google to verify if the channel had initially published the video. The search led the Desk to a video (identical to the viral post) published by Aaj Tak on February 7, 2025. According to the details, the video showed an incident from February 2025, when a frontline twin-seater Mirage-2000 fighter jet of the Indian Air Force crashed at Shivpuri near Gwalior in Madhya Pradesh. Here is the link to the original video, along with a screenshot: Below is a comparison image showing that the content seen in the viral video matches the footage posted by the Facebook page. The customised keyword search also led the Desk to a Times of India report published on February 7, 2025, regarding the same incident. The report stated: "The Mirage-2000, which had taken off from the Gwalior airbase, developed 'a system technical malfunction' and then crashed around 2:40 pm. The two pilots managed to eject safely." Here is the link to the report, along with a screenshot: Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the viral video was unrelated to any military conflict between India and Pakistan and was falsely linked to Operation Sindoor.

author: Kaushiki Goel/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: 2019 photo of MiG-21 crash falsely shared as recent image from Operation Sindoor
content: New Delhi, May 9 (Kaushiki Goel / Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): Following India's precision strikes under Operation Sindoor, which reportedly killed 100 terrorists in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, several social media users shared a photo of a wrecked aircraft part, claiming that the Indian Army had acknowledged the destruction of three of its aircraft. However, the PTI Fact Check Desk investigated and found that the image was shared with a misleading claim. The photograph is from 2019 and has no connection to Operation Sindoor. According to official sources, Operation Sindoor is still underway, making it difficult to provide an exact number of casualties or damage. The government has also stated that India will not initiate any further action unless provoked by Pakistan. Claim A photo of a part of a wrecked aircraft was shared by an X user named 'S2FUncensored' on May 7, claiming that the Indian Army admitted to the downing of three aircraft. The user linked it to Operation Sindoor. "The Indian Army admits to the downing of three aircraft, including Rafale jets, one Su-30, and one MiG-29," read the caption, which clocked 14.7k views. Here is the link and archive link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. Investigation The Desk ran the viral photo through Reverse Image Search and found several other users shared the same photo with a similar claim on social media. Two such posts can be found here and here , along with their archived version, which can be viewed here and here , respectively. On further scanning the search results, the Desk came across the same image published in a news report by DNA along with several other pictures on February 28, 2019, making it clear that the incident pre-dates Operation Sindoor. According to the report, the wing commander, whose MiG 21 Bison aircraft was shot down by the Pakistan Air Force, ejected safely but landed across the Line of Control and was taken into custody by the Pakistan Army. "Abhinandan Varthaman released: All you need to know about IAF Pilot who comes from a long line of 'faujis'," read the headline of the report. Here is the link to the report, and below is a screenshot of the same. Below is a combination image highlighting the social media post's content, matched with the picture in DNA's news report. Taking a cue from this, the Desk conducted a customised keyword search on Google to find other relevant media reports and found a Press Trust of India (PTI) report by NDTV published on March 3, 2019. As per the report, Indian Air Force pilot Abhinandan Varthaman, who was captured by Pakistan when he crossed the Line of Control chasing a Pak F-16 fighter jet, crossed the Attari-Wagah border around 9.20 pm (March 1, 2019), about three hours after he was reportedly scheduled to return. "The confrontation erupted in the days following the February 14 Pulwama attack by Pakistan-based terror group Jaish-e-Mohammed, in which over 40 soldiers were killed. India's air strikes on Tuesday targeted a huge Jaish training facility in Pakistan's Balakot," read a section of the report. Here is the link to the report, and below is a screenshot of the same. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the viral photograph is of a MiG 21 Bison aircraft and it dates back to 2019. An old and unrelated picture was shared recently, linking it to Operation Sindoor.

author: Kaushiki Goel/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: 2024 video of massive fire falsely shared to claim Pakistan attacked military base in Amritsar
content: New Delhi, May 9 (Kaushiki Goel / Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): Since the launch of Operation Sindoor, several pieces of misleading information have surfaced online. One such video, depicting a massive fire followed by a blast, is being circulated on social media with the false claim that Pakistan struck a military base in Amritsar, resulting in numerous casualties. However, the Press Trust of India's (PTI) Fact Check Desk investigated and found that the viral video actually dates back to 2024 and shows wildfires in Chile that killed at least 51 people. The video predates Operation Sindoor and was falsely shared on social media with a misleading claim. Claim A video featuring a massive fire followed by a blast was shared by an X user named RashiD AfriDi on May 8, claiming that Pakistan struck a military base in Amritsar, which led to numerous casualties. "Pakistan strikes military base in Amritsar. Numerous casualties reported, with several critically injured," read the post's caption with 1,235 views. Here is the link and archive link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. Investigation The Desk ran the viral video through the InVid verification tool and extracted multiple keyframes. One of these keyframes was reverse-searched using Google Lens, which led the Desk to several social media posts sharing the same video with similar claims. One such post can be found here , and its archived version can be viewed here . On further scanning the search results, the Desk came across a Facebook post dated February 4, 2024, by a user named 'Acción Ciudadana Chile'. According to the user, the visuals of fire from Valparaiso in Chile. The visuals were the same as seen in the viral post. Here is the link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. The Desk also came across a report by The Times of Israel published on April 14, 2024, predating Operation Sindoor. The report's feature image was similar to the various clips seen in the viral footage. According to the report, it was footage of a fire in Chile. "Iran state TV airs clip of blaze in Chile, claims it shows destruction in Israel," read the headline of the report. Here is the link to the report, and below is a screenshot of the same. The Desk then conducted a customised keyword search on Google to find relevant reports and came across a CNN video report that showed a raging wildfire in Chile. The video was uploaded on February 5, 2024. Here is the link to the report, and below is a screenshot of the same. Another report was published by Reuters on February 4, 2024, mentioning that forest fires raging in central Chile killed at least 51 people. Here is the link to the report. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the viral video dates back to 2024 during the raging wildfires in Chile and is unrelated to Pakistan's military strike in Amritsar airbase.

author: Kaushiki Goel/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: 2024 video of Hezbollah rocket attack falsely shared as Pakistan's strike on Amritsar intercepted by India
content: New Delhi, May 9 (Kaushiki Goel / Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): After India neutralised Pakistan's air defence system in Lahore in retaliation for drone and military attacks in the northern and western regions on the night of May 7 (Wednesday), a video showing rockets being launched into the sky was widely shared on social media. Users claimed the footage showed missiles fired by Pakistan towards Amritsar, which were intercepted by India's air defence systems. However, the Press Trust of India's (PTI) Fact Check Desk investigated and found the video dates back to 2024 and is unrelated to Operation Sindoor. It actually shows Hezbollah rockets being fired at Israeli communities. The video was falsely shared on social media with a misleading claim. Notably, since the launch of Operation Sindoor, India has deployed a range of advanced, long-range precision strike weapons, including the SCALP cruise missile, HAMMER precision-guided bombs, loitering munitions, the Integrated Counter-UAS Grid, Harpy drones, and the S-400 Sudarshan Chakra air defence system. Claim: An X user named Shweta Gupta shared a video on May 8, 2025, of what looked like rockets being fired into the air at night. The user claimed that they were missiles fired by Pakistan in Amritsar, which were intercepted by Indian Air Defence. "Pakistan attack on Amritsar airbase, but Indian Air defence intercepted several Pakistani missiles," read the post's caption, which hit 636 views. Here is the link and archive link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. Investigation: The Desk ran the viral video through the InVid verification tool and extracted multiple keyframes. One of these keyframes was reverse-searched using Google Lens, which led the Desk to several social media posts sharing the same video with similar claims. One such post can be found here , and its archived version can be viewed here . On further scanning the search results, the Desk came across an X-post dated August 4, 2024 (making it clear that it is unrelated to Operation Sindoor), by the official X account of Israel. The video in the post was similar to the one seen in the viral post. The official X account reported that a barrage of Hezbollah rockets was fired at Israeli communities. "Last night in northern Israel: a barrage of Hezbollah rockets fired at Israeli communities. We will not allow Hezbollah, Hamas or any other Iranian proxy to harm the people of Israel." Here is the link and archive link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. Below is a combination image highlighting the viral video's content, matched with the video posted on Israel's official X account. Taking a cue from this, the Desk conducted a customised keyword search on Google to find relevant media reports citing the same incident. We found a video report uploaded on the official YouTube channel of the Associated Press on August 4, 2024. According to the report, Israel's Iron Dome air defence system fired to intercept an attack from Lebanon over the Galilee region in the early hours of Sunday. Here is the link to the report, and below is a screenshot of the same. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the viral video dates back to 2024 when a barrage of Hezbollah rockets was fired at Israeli communities. The video is old and unrelated to any recent happenings.

author: Vaidehi Jahagirdar/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: Old image from Gaza falsely shared to claim Pakistan launched airstrike in Jammu
content: New Delhi, May 9 (Vaidehi Jahagirdar / Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): An image purportedly taken at night, showing smoke rising from an unidentified location, was recently shared on social media with the claim that it depicted the aftermath of a Pakistani retaliatory airstrike that caused significant damage to the Indian Air Force base in Jammu. However, in its investigation, the PTI Fact Check Desk found the image to be unrelated to the ongoing military tensions between India and Pakistan, which escalated following the Pahalgam terror attack that claimed the lives of 26 individuals, mostly tourists. The image in question was actually from Gaza and originally depicted the aftermath of Israeli airstrikes carried out there in September 2021. It is important to note that, in response to the Pahalgam terror attack, Indian armed forces conducted precision strikes across nine locations in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, targeting terrorist infrastructure believed to have been used to plan and direct attacks against India. These military actions were carried out under 'Operation Sindoor'. Claim An X user, Ali Hassan (@AliHassanHQ), shared an image on May 8 claiming that it depicted the aftermath of a Pakistani retaliatory airstrike which caused multiple impacts on the Indian Air Force Base in Jammu. "Pakistan has retaliated! Multiple impacts on Indian Air Force Base in Jammu," the post read. Here is the link and archive link to the post, along with a screenshot: Investigation The Desk ran the viral photo through Reverse Image Search and found several other users shared the same photo with similar claims. One such post can be found here , with its archived version available here : Further, a Google reverse image search led the Desk to a report published by Al Jazeera on its Arabic website (aljazeera.net), where the featured image exactly matched the one now being shared in the social media posts. Upon closely reviewing the Al Jazeera report, the Desk found that the image actually depicted scenes from Gaza after a series of Israeli airstrikes conducted there in September 2021. The image has no connection to the current India-Pakistan situation. "The Israeli military said that, based on an assessment of the security situation, it had decided to reinforce the Gaza Division with additional forces, revealing that it had bombed four Hamas sites in response to incidents in northern Gaza," the report stated. Here is the link to the Al Jazeera report, along with a screenshot: A combination image created by the Desk shows the match between the viral image and the original image from the Al Jazeera report. To verify whether Pakistan had in fact carried out airstrikes on Indian military bases, the Desk conducted a keyword search on Google. The results led to a social media post from the official X handle of the Headquarters Integrated Defence Staff (HQ IDS). According to the post, Pakistan did target military stations in Jammu, Pathankot, and Udhampur using missiles and drones. However, the Indian Armed Forces successfully neutralised the threats and reported no losses. "Military stations of Jammu, Pathankot and Udhampur in proximity to the International Boundary in Jammu & Kashmir were targeted by Pakistan using missiles and drones. No losses. Threat neutralised by #IndianArmedForces as per SoP with kinetic & non-kinetic means," the statement from HQ IDS read. Here is the link to the official post, along with a screenshot: Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the social media image is unrelated to the ongoing India-Pakistan tensions and was originally taken in Gaza during Israeli airstrikes in September 2021.

author: Kaushiki Goel/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: 2019 video of injured pilot shared as recent incident to falsely claim 'Pakistan captured Indian pilot
content: New Delhi, May 9 (Kaushiki Goel / Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): As India launched Operation Sindoor in the early hours of May 7, targeting terrorist infrastructure at nine locations across Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir, social media has been flooded with videos, many of them false or misleading, claiming to depict the current situation. One such video was widely shared by users, falsely claiming that an Indian pilot had been captured after Pakistan shot down his plane. However, the Press Trust of India's (PTI) Fact Check Desk investigated and found that the viral video actually dates back to 2019, when two Surya Kiran Aerobatic Team aircraft collided mid-air and crashed during a practice sortie in Bengaluru. The video was falsely circulated as recent and linked to the ongoing border tensions. Notably, Pakistani troops resumed firing across the Line of Control (LoC), including in the Kupwara and Uri sectors, early Friday (May 9) morning. This followed the Indian Army's successful interception of Pakistani attempts to target 15 cities in northern and western India using drones and missiles on Thursday night (May 8). Claim A video of an injured pilot lying on the ground with a parachute attached to the Overall was shared by an X (formerly Twitter) user named '@mazen00711' on May 9, 2025. The user claimed that an Indian pilot was captured after Pakistan shot down his plane. "Indian pilot captured after Pakistan shot down his plane," read the post's caption, which clocked 58.4k views. Here is the link and archive link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. Investigation The Desk ran the viral video through the InVid verification tool and extracted multiple keyframes. One of these keyframes was reverse-searched using Google Lens, which led the Desk to several social media posts sharing the same video with similar claims. One such post can be found here , and its archived version can be viewed here . The Desk extracted the keyframes of the viral video, ran it through Reverse Image Search, and found a Facebook post dated February 2019. This makes it clear that the video is unrelated to the recent tensions at the border. The post featured the same video as shared on social media. The title of the report read: "Unknown Man Reassured and Holds Hand of Injured Pilot" Here is the link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. Based on the above findings, the Desk conducted a customised keyword search on Google to find relevant media reports. I came across a video report uploaded on YouTube by TV9Kannada dated February 19, 2019. According to the report, the local rescued one of the pilots suffering grievous injuries after 2 Surya Kiran Jets crashed in Bengaluru. The report also showed the same visuals circulated on social media as the recent incident. Here is the link to the report, and below is a screenshot of the same. To find further details of the crash, the Desk again conducted customised keyword searches and came across a report by the Times of India dated February 20, 2019. According to the article, two Surya Kiran Aerobatic Team aircraft collided mid-air and crashed during a practice sortie for the 12th edition of Aero India, casting a shadow on the five-day biennial airshow in Bengaluru. Here is the link to the report. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the viral video of an injured pilot dates back to 2019 when two Surya Kiran Aerobatic Team aircraft collided mid-air and crashed during a practice sortie. It's old and unrelated to the ongoing border tensions following the Pahalgam terror attack or Operation Sindoor.

author: Kaushiki Goel/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: Video of April fire at Dilli Haat falsely shared as Pakistan's attack in India; details inside
content: New Delhi, May 9 (Kaushiki Goel / Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): In the aftermath of the Pahalgam terror attack, which claimed the lives of 26 civilians in Jammu and Kashmir, the Indian Armed Forces launched successful strikes on nine terror targets. Following this, a user shared a video from a leading Hindi news channel, falsely claiming that Pakistani armed forces had attacked Dilli Haat, causing a fire, and linking the incident to ongoing hostilities. However, the Press Trust of India's (PTI) Fact Check Desk investigated the claim and found that the fire at Dilli Haat occurred on April 30, well before Indian forces carried out Operation Sindoor on May 7. The incident is unrelated to the recent border tensions and was shared with a false claim on social media. Claim: An X user named 'Noor' on May 8 shared a video of a news report from a leading Hindi news channel. The anchor could be heard saying that a major fire had been reported from Delhi's prominent market, Delhi Haat. The user claimed that it had been caused by the Pakistani armed forces, linking it to the ongoing hostilities between the two countries at the border. "Delhi is burning. Pakistan armed forces have done it. #PakistanZindabad," read the post's caption. Here is the link and archive link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. Investigation: The Desk ran the viral video through the InVid verification tool and extracted multiple keyframes. One of these keyframes was reverse-searched using Google Lens, which led the Desk to several social media posts sharing the same video with similar claims. One such post can be found here and here , and its archived version can be viewed here and here . To commence the investigation, the Desk extracted the keyframes of the video and ran them through Reverse Image Search to find the original news clip. The search led us to the NDTV report of the fire incident at Dilli Haat, published on April 30, 2025 – making it clear that the incident has no relation with the current situation and Pakistan's retaliation. According to the article, a major fire broke out at a popular art and craft market in Delhi on Wednesday evening (April 30). No injuries were reported in the fire. "The fire has been doused now, informed Delhi Tourism Minister Kapil Mishra in a post on X at 9.51 pm. There are no reports of any casualties in the fire. I am going to Delhi Haat, he said," read the report. Here is the link to the report, and below is a screenshot of the same. Taking a cue from this, the Desk then conducted a customised keyword search to find relevant articles that reported the incident. Our search led us to a report by The Times of India published on May 2, 2025. According to the report, a massive fire broke out at Delhi's popular Dilli Haat market in the INA area on the evening of April 30, 2025, causing significant damage to numerous stalls and shops. "The blaze erupted around 8:55 PM, prompting an immediate response from the Delhi Fire Service, which deployed 14 fire engines to the scene. Fortunately, no casualties have been reported," read a section of the report. Here is the link to the report, and below is a screenshot of the same. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the viral video of the news report is of when fire broke out in Dilli Haat on April 30, 2025. It is unrelated to Pakistan's attack.

author: Kaushiki Goel/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: PTI Fact Check: 2023 photo of Crimea airfield explosion shared to falsely claim 'Indian air defence system was hit in Adampur'
content: New Delhi, May 9 (Kaushiki Goel / Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): Amid the ongoing India-Pakistan military conflict, several social media users shared a photo showing a large explosion with a massive fireball and a dense cloud of smoke, claiming it depicted a missile strike on an Indian S-400 air defence system site in Adampur. However, the Press Trust of India's (PTI) Fact Check Desk investigated and found that the viral photo actually dates back to 2023 and shows an explosion at an airfield in Crimea. The image is unrelated to the current conflict and was shared online with a false claim. Notably, the Ministry of Defence has granted the Army Chief expanded authority to mobilise the Territorial Army amid escalating tensions with Pakistan. This follows the launch of 'Operation Sindoor' by the Indian Armed Forces, which killed over 100 terrorists in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. In retaliation, Pakistan launched missiles and drones across the Line of Control and international borders, all of which were intercepted by India's air defence systems. Claim A user named Jamshaid shared an image on X (formerly Twitter) on May 8, 2025, depicting a large explosion with a massive fireball and a dense cloud of smoke rising into the sky. The user claimed that a missile had hit the Indian S-400 air defence system site in Adampur. "Indian S-400 air defence system site in Adampur hit by unknown missiles and drones," read the post's caption, which clocked 1,158 views. Here is the link and archive link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. Investigation The Desk ran the viral photo through Google Lens and found that several users had shared the same photo with a similar claim on social media. Two such posts can be found here and here , along with their archived version, which can be viewed here and here , respectively. On further scanning the search results, the Desk came across a report by RBC Ukraine, a Ukrainian news agency, published on July 26, 2024. The report clarified that the photo is not from India or its Air Defence being struck by missiles. According to the report, the satellite images were of the aftermath of the explosions at the airfield in Crimea. "Consequences of explosions at the airfield in Crimea: satellite images," read the title of the report. Here is the link to the report, and below is a screenshot of the same. Below is a combination image highlighting the similarities between the viral photo and the news report. Taking a cue from this, the Desk conducted a customised keyword search to find other media reports citing the incident. Our search led us to a report by CNN published on July 20, 2023. According to the report, a series of explosions were reported at a Russian ammunition dump in occupied Crimea, forcing thousands of people to evacuate and prompting leaders there to redirect traffic. Russian President Vladimir Putin was briefed on the explosions. "According to Sergey Aksyonov, the Russian-backed leader of Crimea, a fire occurred at a military training ground. According to Russian state media, the head of Crimea's parliament said it could take two days to fully extinguish the blaze," read a section of the report. Here is the link to the report, and below is a screenshot of the same. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the viral photo dates back to 2023 and depicts an explosion at the airfield in Crimea. It is unrelated to the ongoing tensions at the border of India and Pakistan.

author: Vaidehi Jahagirdar/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: Old Ukraine video shared to falsely claim 'Adampur military base damaged in Pakistani airstrike'
content: New Delhi, May 10 (Vaidehi Jahagirdar / Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): Several social media users recently shared an image claiming it showed a key military installation in Punjab's Adampur that was damaged in a purported Pakistani airstrike on India. However, the Press Trust of India's (PTI) Fact Check Desk investigated the claim and found the image to be unrelated to the ongoing military tensions between India and Pakistan, which escalated after the Pahalgam terror attack that claimed the lives of 26 individuals, mostly tourists. The image in question actually shows Russian S-400 launch units destroyed in Ukrainian airstrikes on Dzhankoi in occupied Crimea. It is important to note that, in response to the Pahalgam terror attack, the Indian Armed Forces conducted precision strikes at multiple locations in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, targeting terrorist infrastructure. These military actions were carried out under 'Operation Sindoor'. Claim An X user, Sam (@x_stoneage), shared an image on May 9, claiming it depicted the aftermath of a Pakistani retaliatory airstrike that caused significant damage to a key military installation in Punjab's Adampur. The user wrote, "Indian officials confirmed that a key military installation in Adampur was hit last night." Here is the link and archive link to the post, along with a screenshot: Investigation The Desk ran the viral image through Google Reverse Image Search and found several other social media handles had shared the same image with similar claims. Two such posts can be found here and here , along with their archived versions viewed here and here , respectively: The reverse image search also led the Desk to a report by The Moscow Times, which featured the same image. The report stated that in April 2024, Ukrainian forces struck a large Russian airfield in the annexed Crimean peninsula, destroying an array of military equipment. "The attack reportedly led to the destruction of radar systems, air defence units, and other military assets," the report added. Here is the link to the report, along with a screenshot: A comparison image created by the Desk shows that the viral image is identical to the original image from the news report. The search result also led the Desk to a related report published by The Eurasian Times on April 18, 2024. Like The Moscow Times, this report confirmed that Russia lost an S-400 surface-to-air missile (SAM) battery in northern Crimea on April 17 to a Ukrainian strike. This further proves that the viral image has no connection to the ongoing tensions between India and Pakistan. Here is the link to the report, along with a screenshot. Further, as part of the investigation, the Desk also conducted a customised keyword search on Google to determine whether any credible reports existed about a Pakistani airstrike destroying a key military installation in India. While the search yielded no credible reports supporting such a claim, it led to a press release issued by the Ministry of Defence on May 8, 2025. The press release stated, "On the night of 07-08 May 2025, Pakistan attempted to engage a number of military targets in Northern and Western India including Awantipura, Srinagar, Jammu, Pathankot, Amritsar, Kapurthala, Jalandhar, Ludhiana, Adampur, Bhatinda, Chandigarh, Nal, Phalodi, Uttarlai, and Bhuj, using drones and missiles. The Integrated Counter UAS Grid and Air Defence systems neutralised these." Here is the link to the press release, along with a screenshot: Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the social media image does not show an Indian military installation in Adampur that suffered damage from a Pakistani retaliatory airstrike.

author: Vaidehi Jahagirdar/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: Old unrelated video shared with the reports of Pakistani missile attack on India; details inside
content: New Delhi, May 10 (Vaidehi Jahagirdar / Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): Multiple social media users recently shared a video claiming it showed Pakistan's Fateh-2 ballistic missile being intercepted by India's 'Barak-8 Missile System' in Sirsa, Haryana. However, in its investigation, the PTI Fact Check Desk found the video unrelated to the ongoing India-Pakistan military conflict. It was uploaded at least four months earlier on a third-party platform. Claim An X user 'Priyanshu Kumar' (@priyanshu__63) shared a video on May 10, allegedly showing Pakistan's Fateh-2 ballistic missile being intercepted by India's Barak-8 missile system in Sirsa, Haryana. The user claimed that the missile was aimed at the national capital, New Delhi, but was intercepted by Indian armed forces. Pakistan tried to hit the capital of India, New Delhi, with its long-range missile Fateh-2. But it was intercepted by the Barak-8 missile defence system in Sirsa of Haryana," the post read. When this article was published, the video had garnered 772k views and 6.8k likes. Here is the link and archive link to the post, along with a screenshot. Investigation The Desk ran the viral video through the InVid tool and extracted multiple keyframes. Running one of the keyframes through Google Lens, the Desk found several other social media accounts that shared the same video with similar claims. Two such posts can be found here and here , with their archived versions viewed here and here , respectively. The search also led the Desk to a video published on Tokyvideo, where the duplicate footage had been uploaded at least four months ago, well before the recent India-Pakistan escalation. According to the description, the video was filmed somewhere in the Middle East; however, the Desk could not independently verify the authenticity of this claim, apart from the fact that it is not related to ongoing tension between India and Pakistan. Here is the link to the video, along with a screenshot. A comparison image created by the Desk confirmed that the viral video matches the footage posted on Tokyvideo. Additionally, as part of the investigation, the Desk also conducted a customised keyword search on Google to check whether Pakistan had attempted an airstrike over Sirsa, Haryana, that was thwarted. The search led to a report by The Indian Express, published on May 10, 2025, covering the incident. The report stated, "An airstrike attempt by Pakistan was thwarted over Sirsa in Haryana. The remnants of missile-like objects were found at two places in the fields of Sirsa, near the Air Force station. Teams of the Indian Air Force and district police reached both locations, collected the debris, and took it away." Here is the link to the report, along with a screenshot. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that amid the reports of a Pakistani airstrike attempt over Sirsa, the video circulated on social media was not related to that event. It was an old video falsely shared in the context of current India-Pakistan military conflict.

author: Vaidehi Jahagirdar/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: Old fire video from Dubai shared to falsely claim Pakistani airstrike damaged Gujarat's Hazira Port; details inside
content: New Delhi, May 10 (Vaidehi Jahagirdar / Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): A video showing destruction caused by a fire at an unidentified location was recently shared on social media with the claim that it depicted the aftermath of a Pakistani retaliatory airstrike that caused significant damage to Gujarat's Hazira Port on May 8. However, the PTI Fact Check Desk found the video unrelated to the ongoing India-Pakistan military conflict. The footage actually showed scenes from Dubai's Jebel Ali Port, where a fire broke out in July 2021 after an explosion within a container on board a ship. An old and unrelated video was falsely circulated on social media with a misleading claim. Claim An X user 'Miss Anaya' (@MissAnaya26) shared a video on May 8, claiming it depicted the aftermath of a Pakistani retaliatory airstrike that caused significant damage to Gujarat's Hazira Port. The user wrote: "India Gujarat Adani-owned multiple missiles have struck Hazira port. Whole port has been destroyed." Here is the link and archive link to the post, along with a screenshot: Investigation The Desk ran the viral video through the InVid tool and extracted multiple keyframes. Running one of the keyframes through Google Lens, the Desk found multiple social media users who had shared the same video with similar claims. One such post can be found here , along with its archived version viewed here respectively: The Google Lens search results also led the Desk to a video published by an X handle named Joe Truzman. The handle had posted the same video as seen in the viral post. Further analysis revealed that the footage dated back to July 2021 and actually depicted scenes from Dubai's Jebel Ali Port, which experienced a fire following an explosion. Here is the link and archive link to the post, along with a screenshot: A comparison image created by the Desk shows that the content in the viral video matches the footage posted by the X handle. In the next phase of the investigation, taking a cue from the findings above, the Desk conducted a customised keyword search on Google regarding the fire incident at Dubai's Jebel Ali Port. The search results led to a report published by the UK-based tabloid The Sun, which featured the same video footage used in the social media post. The report stated that the fire was caused by an explosion within a container on board a ship at Jebel Ali Port in July 2021. Here is the link to the report, along with a screenshot: Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the viral video does not depict damage caused at Gujarat's Hazira Port due to a Pakistani airstrike.

author: Vaidehi Jahagirdar/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: Old fire video from Gurugram resurfaced to falsely claim Pakistani missile strike happened there; details inside
content: New Delhi, May 10 (Vaidehi Jahagirdar / Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): Amid heightened military tensions between India and Pakistan following the Pahalgam terror attack, a video showing a fire at an unidentified location was recently shared on social media with the claim that it depicted the aftermath of a Pakistani missile strike on Gurugram. The user alleged that the missile attack had triggered a massive blaze in the area. However, upon investigation, the PTI Fact Check Desk found that the video is unrelated to the ongoing India-Pakistan conflict. The footage actually shows a fire that broke out near the Basai Chowk area in Gurugram on March 29. Around 100 shanties were destroyed in the blaze, which was reportedly caused by a gas cylinder explosion. An old video was falsely shared on social media with a misleading claim. Claim: A Facebook page named Express Pakistan shared a video on May 8, claiming it showed the aftermath of a Pakistani missile attack on Gurugram. The post alleged that the incident triggered a massive fire in the region. Here is the link and archive link to the post, along with a screenshot. Investigation: The Desk used the InVid tool to extract multiple keyframes from the viral video. Running one of the keyframes through Google Lens, the Desk discovered several other users had shared the same video with similar claims. Two such posts can be found here and here , with their archived versions viewed here and here , respectively: The reverse image search also led the Desk to a video posted by an Instagram page named gurgaon_culture. The page had shared the same footage as seen in the social media video on March 29, 2025, predating the current military conflict. The post further clearly stated that the video showed a fire incident at Basai Chowk in Gurugram. Here is the link and archive link to the post, along with a screenshot. A comparison image confirms that the content in the viral video matches the original footage shared on the Instagram handle. Additionally, as part of the investigation, the Desk conducted a customised keyword search on Google regarding the Basai Chowk fire incident to verify the context further. This led the Desk to a report published by Amar Ujala, which featured a video that showed the same footage as that of the viral clip, but was shot from a different angle. The report stated that around 100 shanties were destroyed in a fire caused by a gas cylinder explosion on March 29. Fortunately, no casualties were reported. Here is the link to the report, along with a screenshot. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the social media video does not depict the aftermath of a Pakistani missile attack on Gurugram. It actually shows a fire incident that occurred on March 29, 2025, near Basai Chowk in Gurugram.

author: Vaidehi Jahagirdar/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: Unrelated, old video shared on social media to falsely claim 'Indian soldiers abandoned their posts amid India-Pak military conflict'
content: New Delhi, May 10 (Vaidehi Jahagirdar/ Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): Amid escalating military tensions between India and Pakistan following the Pahalgam terror attack, a video allegedly showing an Indian Army personnel getting emotional has been widely shared on social media. Users circulating the clip claimed that the soldier was crying due to the intensifying conflict on the ground. They claimed that as the India-Pakistan war intensified, Indian soldiers abandoned their posts. However, a PTI Fact Check Desk investigation has found that the video is unrelated to the current military situation. It actually shows students from a private defence coaching institute in Indore who became emotional after receiving news of their selection into the Indian Army. Claim On May 9, an X user named 'Mr. Sunatan' (@hot_soup333) shared a video, claiming it depicted an Indian soldier being overwhelmed by escalating military conflict between India and Pakistan. "As the India-Pakistan war intensifies, Indian soldiers are being seen crying and abandoning their posts. 'This isn't what we signed up for,' says one soldier," the post read. At the time of publishing, the video had garnered over 61,000 views. Here is the link and archive link to the post, along with a screenshot. Investigation The Desk used the InVid tool to extract multiple keyframes from the viral video. Running one of the keyframes through Google Lens, the Desk discovered another social media user who had shared the same video with similar claim. The post can be found here , with its archived version viewed here respectively. The reverse image search also led the Desk to a video published on an Instagram page named 'indore_physical_academy01'. The page featured the same individuals seen in the viral clip. The background setting and events depicted in the video matched those in the viral footage. However, upon further analysis, the Desk found that the video was originally shared on the Instagram page on April 27, 2025—well before military tensions between the two nations escalated on May 7, when India launched Operation Sindoor, targeting multiple terror-linked infrastructures in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. Here is the link and archive link to the video, along with a screenshot. A comparison image confirms that the content in the viral video matches the original footage shared on the Instagram handle. In the subsequent part of the investigation, to verify the claim made in the viral post, the Desk contacted the phone number provided on the Instagram page 'indore_physical_academy01'. Upon speaking with a representative, it was confirmed that the video shows students from a private defence coaching institute celebrating their selection into the Indian Army. "This video is four years old. Some of our students had become soldiers at that time, and they became emotional upon hearing the news, which led to the making of the video," an official from the academy told the PTI Fact Check Desk. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the video was unrelated to the ongoing military conflict. Instead, it depicted students from a private defence coaching institute reacting emotionally after learning about their selection into the Indian Army.

author: Vaidehi Jahagirdar/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: It's CHEAPFAKE! AI-generated video of EAM Jaishankar shared with false, fabricated, baseless claims; details inside
content: New Delhi, May 10 (Vaidehi Jahagirdar/Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): In the wake of the recent India-Pakistan military conflict, a video purportedly showing External Affairs Minister Dr. S. Jaishankar apologising to the world surfaced online. The video appeared to depict the Minister admitting that India had falsely accused Pakistan of being behind the Pahalgam terror attack. It also showed him claiming that India is now seeking an apology from the global community after facing the consequences of its alleged deceit. However, the PTI Fact Check Desk found the video to be doctored and falsely circulated on social media to mislead viewers. Claim An X user, Abubakar Qassam (@abubakarqassam), shared a video on May 10 claiming to show External Affairs Minister Dr. S. Jaishankar apologising to the world. The video appeared to show the Minister admitting that India had falsely accused Pakistan of being the perpetrator behind the Pahalgam terror attack. Here is the link and archive link to the post, along with a screenshot. When this story was published, the video had garnered 328.4K views and 2.6K likes. Investigation As part of the investigation, the Desk carefully analysed the viral video and found multiple inconsistencies. For example, the Minister's lip movements were distorted and not synchronised with the speech. Additionally, his facial expressions looked unnatural, raising suspicions that the video was AI-generated. Below is a screenshot highlighting the key findings. In the next phase of the investigation, the Desk ran the video through the InVid tool using the initial observations and extracted multiple keyframes. The Desk ran four of these keyframes through Hive Moderation, an AI detection tool, one by one. The results indicated that all of them contained deepfake or AI-generated content. Below are screenshots of the keyframes analysed using Hive Moderation: Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the video shared on social media, showing the External Affairs Minister extending an apology, was AI-generated.

author: Kaushiki Goel/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: China Daily's X handle shared 2019 photo of Mi-17 crash to falsely claim three Indian jets crashed in Kashmir during recent India-Pakistan conflict
content: New Delhi, May 11 (Kaushiki Goel / Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): The official X handle of China Daily, a China-based English news outlet, recently shared a post claiming that three Indian military jets had crashed in Jammu and Kashmir on Wednesday (May 7) during the recent India-Pakistan military conflict. Following this, multiple social media users circulated an image purportedly showing the aftermath of the alleged crash. However, the PTI Fact Check Desk investigated the claim and found it false. The image being shared was actually from February 2019, when an Indian Air Force Mi-17 helicopter crashed in Budgam, Jammu and Kashmir, after an Indian missile mistakenly hit it. The photo used in the China Daily X post is old, and there has been no official confirmation of any Indian jet crashes in Kashmir on May 7. Claim An X (formerly Twitter) post shared by China Daily, a China-based English Daily, shared a picture showing the aftermath of a military aircraft crash. The post, citing The Hindu, claimed that three Indian jets crashed on Wednesday in Indian-controlled Kashmir. "At least three #Indian jets crashed Wednesday in Indian-controlled #Kashmir, a local newspaper The Hindu said quoting government sources. #Pakistan," read the post's caption, Here is the link and archive link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. Investigation The Desk ran the viral photo through Google Lens and came across several users who shared the same photo with a similar claim shared on social media. Two such posts can be found here and here , and their archived versions can be viewed here and here , respectively. Upon scanning the search results further, the Desk found a Press Trust of India (PTI) report from Kashmir Observer dated September 14, 2020. The article's cover image was similar to the one shared by China Daily on the X platform. According to the report, the Mi-17 helicopter was shot down by a missile in Kashmir's Budgam on February 27, 2019. The headline read: "Budgam Mi-17 Crash: Tribunal Stays Action Against 2 IAF Officers" Here is the link to the report, and below is a screenshot of the same. Though the picture used in the report was not detailed, it is clear that it is not recent and has been available on the internet at least since 2020. Taking a cue from the above finding that the incident occurred in 2019, the Desk conducted customised keyword searches on Google to find relevant media reports. We found another Press Trust of India (PTI) report carried by the Economic Times on August 23, 2019. The cover image used in the report had striking similarities with the viral picture. As per the article, the Mi-17 IAF helicopter that crashed in Budgam in Jammu and Kashmir on February 27, the day Indian and Pakistani air forces were engaged in a fierce dogfight, was hit by an Indian missile, according to a high-level probe that found at least four officers guilty. Six military personnel and a civilian were killed in the incident. At least four officers, including a group captain, were held responsible for the crash of the chopper in the friendly fire and are set to face severe punishment, military sources said on Friday," read a section of the report. Here is the link to the report, and below is a screenshot of the same. Below is a combination image highlighting the similarities between the viral photo and the news report's feature image. The investigation has revealed that the photo has been on the internet since 2019. This clarifies that it does not depict the incident of the Indian aircraft crash during Operation Sindoor. The China Daily quoted The Hindu as the source of the news piece. Desk then looked for reports by The Hindu and found that it had posted on X on May 7, 2025, mentioning that three jets crashed in the Akhnoor, Ramban, and Pampore areas. The post now stands deleted; however, China Daily has not yet retracted or edited its X post following the developments by The Hindu. The Desk came across the screenshot of The Hindu post shared by an X user on social media. Below is a screenshot of the same. Hours after the post, The Hindu issued a clarification on X that there was no on-record official information about the crash of an Indian aircraft and that they had deleted the earlier post. "We have deleted an earlier post about Indian aircraft involved in Operation Sindoor. There is no official information from India on record. We therefore decided to remove the post from our platforms. We regret that it created confusion among our readers," read the post, dated May 7, 2025. Here is the link to the post, and below is a screenshot of the same. ​ Furthermore, during the press briefing on May 10, 2025, Colonel Sofiya Qureshi debunked Pakistan's misinformation campaign. "First, Pakistan falsely claimed that it had damaged India's S-400 system and BrahMos missile base using its JF-17 aircraft; this is completely untrue. Second, the claim that our airfields in Sirsa, Jammu, Pathankot, Bathinda, Naliya, and Bhuj were hit is false. Third, Pakistan's assertion that our ammunition dumps in Chandigarh and Beas were damaged is yet another baseless claim," she said. Here is the link to the X post by Press Trust of India, and below is a screenshot of the same. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the photo in the social media post was unrelated to the recent India-Pakistan military conflict.

author: Kaushiki Goel/Pratyush Ranjan
title: PTI Fact Check: Fabricated press release, old image used to falsely claim former Pak PM Imran Khan's death
content: New Delhi, May 11 (Kaushiki Goel / Pratyush Ranjan, PTI Fact Check ): A purported picture of former Pakistan Prime Minister and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) chief Imran Khan, showing him with head injuries and bleeding, was shared on social media, with users claiming that he had been killed by the ISI. The claim was further fueled by an alleged press release from the Government of Pakistan announcing Khan's death. However, the Press Trust of India's (PTI) Fact Check Desk investigated and found that the image of an injured Imran Khan dates back to 2013, when he fell from a lift carrying him to a stage approximately 10–14 feet high at a rally in Lahore. Upon further investigation, the press release was found to be forged, fabricated, and digitally altered. The social media posts were thus shared with a false claim. According to official records, Imran Khan is currently lodged in Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail, serving sentences in multiple cases, including corruption and unlawful marriage. Senior leaders from Khan's party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, have expressed growing concern over his health and safety, alleging that he is being held in near-isolation with restricted access to medical care and legal counsel. Claim A purported picture of former Pakistan PM Imran Khan injured and being carried by a few men was shared by an X user, 'Jitendra pratap singh', on May 10, claiming that he was killed by ISI. The user in another post shared an alleged press release claiming it to be the official release from the Government of Pakistan, citing Khan's death. "Imran Khan has been killed by ISI. They are hiding this news so it doesn't create a Civil war inside Pakistan. Please spread this news," read the post's caption, which clocked 76k views. Here are the first link and second link , along with the first archive link and second archive link to the posts. Below is a screenshot of the same. Investigation The Desk ran Imran Khan's viral image through Reverse Image Search and found that several other users had shared the same picture along with a similar claim on social media. Two such posts can be found here and here , and their archived versions can be found here and here , respectively. The Desk first debunked the alleged Press Release from the Government of Pakistan, on careful analysis of the release, the Desk found some discrepancies hinting that it might be fabricated or manipulated. The date in the top right corner appeared to be hidden, with only 2025 written. Also, there was no signature or name of the authority issuing it mentioned– it only mentioned 'Islamabad', which is vague. We also noticed a typo in the letter, hinting that it could not be an official release. Below is a screenshot highlighting the same. In the next part of the investigation, the Desk checked the official website of Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Government of Pakistan for a press release, but there was no official announcement mentioning the incident. Here is the link , and below is a screenshot of the same. Taking cue from the above findings, the Desk then ran the alleged press release through Hive Moderation (an AI-detection tool). The results indicated that it contained deep fake or AI-generated content. Below is the screenshot of the keyframes analysed using Hive Moderation: It is clear that the release has been digitally altered, as there is no official press release on the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Government of Pakistan's website. In the next part of the investigation, the Desk debunked the picture of the former Pakistan PM being shared on social media. The Desk ran the image through Google Lens and found the same image being used in a news report by India Today published in May 22, 2013. According to India Today, the image is a still from video footage of Imran Khan being rushed to a hospital. It further mentioned that the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), fell off a lift carrying him to a 10-14 feet high stage at a rally in Lahore and sustained head injuries. "He received head injuries and was rushed to a nearby hospital for treatment. According to eyewitnesses, Imran, flanked by his bodyguards, lost balance and fell off the lift that was carrying him onto the stage at Ghalib market where he was to address thousands of party workers and supporters who had gathered for the rally," read a section of the report. Here is the link to the report, and below is a screenshot of the same. The image used in the report had striking similarities with the one being recently shared on social media. Below is a combination image highlighting the similarities between the viral photo and the feature image of India Today report. Since the India Today report mentioned that the cover image they used was a still from video footage, the Desk then conducted another set of customised keyword search on Google to find the video. The search led us to a report by Al Jazeera English published on their official YouTube channel on May 7, 2013. The report mentioned that the cricketer turned politician fell 14 feet as he was stepping off an improvised fork lift that was raising him to the top of the platform "Imran Khan, the chairman of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaaf political party, has been injured after falling from a makeshift stage during a campaign rally in Lahore. The cricketer turned politician fell 14 feet as he was stepping off an improvised fork lift that was raising him to the top of the platform. Local TV station Geo TV aired footage of the accident and showed Khan bleeding and unconscious with a gash on his head," read the report. In the 1 minute 47 seconds video report the exact clip of Imran Khan being carried could be seen at 00:18 seconds timestamp. Here is the link to the report and below is a screenshot of the same. In the subsequent part of the investigation, PTI Fact Check contacted Lubna Jerar Naqvi, a Karachi-based freelance journalist regarding the claim viral on social media. She told PTI Fact Check: "Spreading false news about a popular leader like Imran Khan at such a sensitive time reveals the mindsets and intent behind this. This May 9 marks two years since Imran Khan was arrested and it is a good time to rile emotions. However, any attempt to cause political strain failed since most of Pakistan and the region are already very tense.
